Octopus

The octopus is a soft-bodied, eight-limbed mollusc of the order Octopoda, within the class Cephalopoda, which also includes squid, cuttlefish and the nautilus. Around 300 species are recognised, distributed in every ocean from intertidal pools to abyssal depths exceeding 4,000 metres. Octopuses are notable among invertebrates for their large brains, distributed nervous systems, rapid colour change and demonstrated problem-solving abilities, and they have become a focus of research in neuroscience, comparative cognition and animal welfare law.

Anatomy

The octopus body consists of a bulbous mantle containing the viscera, a head bearing two large eyes, and eight arms joined at the base by a web of skin. The mantle encloses the gills, three hearts and the reproductive and digestive organs. Two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, while a systemic heart circulates it to the rest of the body. The blood contains the copper-based pigment haemocyanin, which gives it a blue colour and is more efficient than haemoglobin in cold, low-oxygen water but less effective in warm conditions.

The only hard part of the body is the chitinous beak, resembling that of a parrot, located at the centre of the arms. Because the beak is the sole rigid structure, an octopus can squeeze through any opening larger than its beak; a 600-gram giant Pacific octopus can pass through a hole roughly 2.5 centimetres across. The arms bear suckers, typically one or two rows, numbering up to about 280 per arm in Octopus vulgaris. Each sucker can be operated independently and carries chemoreceptors, allowing the animal to taste what it touches. The radula, a toothed ribbon in the mouth, works with the beak and salivary enzymes to bore into shells and inject venom.

Locomotion is achieved by crawling with the arms or by jet propulsion, in which water drawn into the mantle cavity is expelled through a muscular siphon. The siphon also expels ink, a suspension of melanin and mucus secreted by the ink sac, used to confuse predators and in some species to dull their sense of smell. Sizes range from the Star-sucker pygmy octopus (Octopus wolfi), with a mantle under 2.5 centimetres and a mass of about one gram, to the giant Pacific octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini), with an average mass of 15 kilograms and arm span of 4.3 metres; the largest reliably measured specimen weighed 71 kilograms.

Nervous system

The octopus nervous system contains roughly 500 million neurons, comparable to that of a dog and far exceeding other invertebrates. Only about a third of these are in the central brain, which is arranged in roughly 30 to 40 lobes around the oesophagus. The remaining two-thirds are distributed in the arms, where ganglia along each arm allow considerable local control. Experiments by Binyamin Hochner and colleagues at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in the 2000s showed that severed arms continue to exhibit coordinated reaching and grasping, and that the brain issues relatively general commands that the arm's own circuitry executes.

The eyes are camera-type, with a lens and retina, an example of convergent evolution with vertebrates; unlike the vertebrate eye, the photoreceptors face the light and there is no blind spot. Most species have a single visual pigment and are presumed colour-blind, although the rectangular pupil may permit chromatic aberration to be exploited for colour discrimination, a hypothesis advanced by Alexander Stubbs and Christopher Stubbs in 2016. Statocysts provide balance and detect low-frequency vibration. The octopus genome, first sequenced for Octopus bimaculoides in 2015 by a team including Caroline Albertin and Clifton Ragsdale, revealed an expanded family of protocadherin genes associated with neural wiring and extensive RNA editing in nervous tissue.

Camouflage

Octopus skin contains three layers of colour-producing structures. Chromatophores are elastic pigment sacs in yellow, red, brown and black, each surrounded by radial muscles under direct neural control, allowing colour change in well under a second. Beneath them lie iridophores, which reflect iridescent blues and greens, and leucophores, which scatter white light and match ambient illumination. Papillae in the skin can be raised to alter texture, mimicking algae, coral or rock.

Roger Hanlon of the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole has documented that octopuses select from a limited set of body patterns—uniform, mottled or disruptive—based on visual assessment of the background. The mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus), described in 1998 from Indonesian waters, imitates the shape and movement of lionfish, sea snakes and flatfish. Some species also display deimatic patterns of high contrast to startle predators. Skin from several species has been shown to contain light-sensitive opsins, suggesting a capacity to detect light directly without the eyes.

Intelligence studies

Laboratory study of octopus learning began in earnest at the Stazione Zoologica in Naples in the 1950s, where J. Z. Young, Brian Boycott and Martin Wells used Octopus vulgaris to investigate memory. Young's work on the vertical lobe established it as a site of learning and influenced theories of neural networks. Octopuses have since been shown to distinguish shapes and brightness, navigate mazes, unscrew jars and solve puzzle boxes. Jennifer Mather and Roland Anderson at the Seattle Aquarium reported in the 1990s that individuals showed consistent temperaments and engaged in apparent play, repeatedly pushing floating bottles into a current.

In 2009, Julian Finn and Mark Norman of Museum Victoria filmed veined octopuses (Amphioctopus marginatus) carrying coconut shell halves across the seabed and assembling them as shelter, which they interpreted as tool use. A 1992 claim by Graziano Fiorito and Pietro Scotto of observational learning between octopuses remains debated. Studies have also documented individuals squirting water at lights or at particular staff members, and the 2016 escape of an octopus named Inky from the National Aquarium of New Zealand through a drain pipe received wide attention. Researchers caution that octopus cognition evolved independently of vertebrate intelligence and may not map onto mammalian categories.

Reproduction and life span

Octopuses are semelparous, reproducing once before dying. The male transfers spermatophores using a modified third right arm, the hectocotylus, which in argonauts and some other species detaches inside the female. The female of Octopus vulgaris lays between 100,000 and 500,000 eggs in strings in a den, aerating and guarding them without feeding for up to a month; giant Pacific octopuses brood for around six months. In 2014 Bruce Robison and colleagues at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute reported a deep-sea Graneledone boreopacifica that brooded a single clutch for 53 months, the longest known for any animal.

After the eggs hatch, the female dies, a process controlled by secretions of the optic glands; Jerome Wodinsky showed in 1977 that removing these glands prolonged life. Males typically die weeks after mating. Most species live one to two years, and the giant Pacific octopus three to five. Hatchlings of most species pass through a planktonic paralarval stage before settling. Cannibalism and sexual cannibalism are recorded in several species.

Species

Major groups include the incirrate octopuses, lacking fins and cirri, and the cirrate or deep-sea finned octopuses such as the dumbo octopuses (Grimpoteuthis). Well-known incirrates include the common octopus (Octopus vulgaris), the blue-ringed octopuses (Hapalochlaena), whose tetrodotoxin has caused human fatalities, and the argonauts (Argonauta), in which the female secretes a thin shell-like egg case. The seven-arm octopus (Haliphron atlanticus) rivals the giant Pacific octopus in mass. Fossil octopuses are rare; Pohlsepia from the Carboniferous and Palaeoctopus from the Cretaceous are among the oldest described.

Relationship with humans

Octopuses have been fished for millennia; Minoan pottery from about 1500 BC depicts them, and they appear in Aristotle's History of Animals. Global catches reported to the FAO have exceeded 350,000 tonnes annually, with major fisheries in Morocco, Mauritania, Mexico, Japan and China, often using clay pots or traps. The Spanish firm Nueva Pescanova announced plans in 2021 for the first commercial octopus farm in the Canary Islands, prompting opposition from scientists and welfare groups citing stress, aggression and proposed slaughter in ice slurry.

Octopuses are kept in public aquariums, where enrichment is required to prevent self-mutilation and escape, and their short lives limit display periods. In 2010 the European Union included cephalopods in Directive 2010/63/EU regulating animal experimentation, the only invertebrates so covered, and in 2022 the United Kingdom's Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act recognised cephalopods as sentient following a review led by Jonathan Birch at the London School of Economics. In 2023 the United States National Institutes of Health sought comment on extending research protections to cephalopods. Debate continues over the ethics of invasive neuroscience and of eating octopus, informed by books such as Peter Godfrey-Smith's Other Minds (2016) and the film My Octopus Teacher (2020).

Tesla, Inc.

Tesla, Inc. is an American electric vehicle and clean energy company headquartered in Austin, Texas. It designs and manufactures battery electric vehicles, stationary battery storage products, solar panels and solar roof tiles, and related software and services. Measured by market capitalization it has been the world's most valuable automaker since 2020, and it was for several years the largest producer of battery electric vehicles by volume. The company is closely identified with its chief executive, Elon Musk, whose public statements and business conduct have repeatedly drawn regulatory and legal scrutiny.

Founding and early years

Tesla Motors was incorporated on July 1, 2003, by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning in San Carlos, California, and named after the inventor Nikola Tesla. Ian Wright joined shortly afterward. In February 2004 Elon Musk led the company's Series A funding round, contributing about 6.5 million dollars of the 7.5 million dollars raised, and became chairman of the board. J. B. Straubel joined as chief technical officer in May 2004. A 2009 lawsuit filed by Eberhard over the right to be called a founder was settled with an agreement that all five men, Eberhard, Tarpenning, Wright, Musk and Straubel, could be described as co-founders.

Eberhard served as chief executive until August 2007, when he was replaced on an interim basis by Michael Marks and then by Ze'ev Drori in December 2007. Musk assumed the role of chief executive in October 2008 amid the financial crisis and a severe cash shortage. The company closed a 40 million dollar debt financing round on Christmas Eve 2008, which Musk later said saved it from bankruptcy. Daimler purchased a stake of roughly 10 percent for 50 million dollars in May 2009, and in January 2010 the United States Department of Energy approved a 465 million dollar loan under the Advanced Technology Vehicles Manufacturing program, repaid in full in May 2013.

Tesla Roadster

The company's first product, the Roadster, was unveiled in July 2006 and entered production in March 2008. It was built on a chassis derived from the Lotus Elise and assembled partly at Lotus's plant in Hethel, England, with final assembly in Menlo Park and later Fremont, California. The car used a 53 kilowatt-hour lithium-ion pack composed of about 6,831 cylindrical 18650 cells and had an EPA range of 244 miles, making it the first production automobile to use lithium-ion cells and the first highway-capable electric car with a range exceeding 200 miles. Priced from about 109,000 dollars, roughly 2,450 units were sold in more than 30 countries before production ended in January 2012. Tesla's initial public offering on the Nasdaq on June 29, 2010, raised 226 million dollars at 17 dollars per share, the first IPO by an American automaker since Ford in 1956.

Model S, Model X, Model 3 and Model Y

In May 2010 Tesla acquired the former NUMMI plant in Fremont, California, from Toyota for 42 million dollars. The Model S, a full-size luxury sedan, began deliveries there in June 2012. It received Motor Trend's Car of the Year award for 2013 and a 99 out of 100 rating from Consumer Reports, and in 2015 and 2016 it was the world's best-selling plug-in car. The Model X, a sport utility vehicle with distinctive upward-opening "falcon wing" rear doors, was delivered from September 2015 after repeated delays.

The Model 3, a smaller sedan intended for the mass market with a base price announced at 35,000 dollars, was unveiled on March 31, 2016, and attracted about 325,000 reservations within a week. Deliveries began in July 2017, but the ramp-up at Fremont, which Musk described as "production hell," fell far short of a target of 5,000 cars per week until mid-2018, during which the company built a temporary assembly line under a tent. The Model 3 became the world's best-selling electric car from 2018 through 2021. The Model Y, a compact crossover sharing about 75 percent of its parts with the Model 3, began deliveries in March 2020 and in 2023 became the best-selling vehicle of any kind worldwide, with about 1.2 million units. The Cybertruck, a stainless-steel pickup unveiled in November 2019, entered limited production in November 2023, and the Semi truck began deliveries in December 2022. Annual deliveries rose from 22,477 in 2013 to 1.31 million in 2022 and 1.81 million in 2023, before declining to 1.79 million in 2024, the company's first annual decrease.

Battery and vehicle factories

In 2014 Tesla announced Gigafactory 1 near Sparks, Nevada, built in partnership with Panasonic to produce cells and battery packs; Nevada granted incentives valued at about 1.3 billion dollars. Gigafactory 2 in Buffalo, New York, makes solar products and was acquired through the 2.6 billion dollar purchase of SolarCity in November 2016, a company chaired by Musk and run by his cousins Lyndon and Peter Rive. Gigafactory Shanghai, Tesla's first wholly foreign-owned car plant in China, began production in late 2019 less than a year after groundbreaking. Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg in Grünheide, Germany, and Gigafactory Texas near Austin both opened in 2022. Tesla has also developed a larger 4680 cylindrical cell format and operates a growing stationary storage business, deploying 31.4 gigawatt-hours of Powerwall and Megapack products in 2024.

Autopilot and investigations

Autopilot, a driver-assistance system combining adaptive cruise control and lane-keeping, was introduced in October 2015 with hardware fitted from September 2014. An expanded "Full Self-Driving" package has been sold since 2016, although it remains a Level 2 system requiring an attentive driver. The first known fatal crash involving Autopilot killed Joshua Brown in Florida in May 2016 when his Model S struck a tractor-trailer. The National Transportation Safety Board investigated that crash and later ones, including the 2018 death of Walter Huang in Mountain View, California, and criticized Tesla for inadequate driver monitoring. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a defect investigation in August 2021 into collisions with stationary emergency vehicles; this led in December 2023 to a recall of about 2.03 million vehicles, addressed through a software update. In 2024 NHTSA opened a further inquiry into Full Self-Driving after a pedestrian death in Arizona. The California Department of Motor Vehicles and the Department of Justice have examined the marketing of the system, and a Florida jury in August 2025 found Tesla partly liable in a 2019 fatal crash and awarded about 243 million dollars.

Financial history

Tesla reported its first quarterly profit in the first quarter of 2013 and its first full-year profit in 2020, when net income reached 721 million dollars on revenue of 31.5 billion dollars. Revenue grew to 96.8 billion dollars in 2023, with net income of 15 billion dollars, before easing to 97.7 billion dollars in revenue and 7.1 billion dollars in net income in 2024. Sales of regulatory credits to other automakers contributed substantially to early profitability. The stock was added to the S&P 500 in December 2020, and the company's market value first exceeded 1 trillion dollars in October 2021. Tesla executed stock splits of 5-for-1 in August 2020 and 3-for-1 in August 2022, and moved its headquarters from Palo Alto to Austin in December 2021.

Lawsuits and leadership controversies

On August 7, 2018, Musk posted on Twitter that he had "funding secured" to take Tesla private at 420 dollars per share. The Securities and Exchange Commission sued him for fraud; in a September 2018 settlement, Musk and Tesla each paid 20 million dollars, Musk resigned as chairman for three years, and Robyn Denholm succeeded him. A shareholder class action over the tweets ended in a jury verdict in Musk's favor in February 2023. In January 2024, Delaware Chancellor Kathaleen McCormick voided Musk's 2018 compensation package, then valued at about 56 billion dollars, ruling the board had not negotiated at arm's length; shareholders reapproved the plan in June 2024, and the company reincorporated in Texas. Tesla has faced numerous workplace suits, including a 2021 verdict of 137 million dollars, later reduced to 3.2 million, for racial harassment of Owen Diaz at Fremont, a 2022 suit by the California Civil Rights Department alleging systemic discrimination, and National Labor Relations Board findings against anti-union conduct. Musk's role in the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency in 2025 prompted protests and vandalism of Tesla showrooms and was linked to a sharp decline in sales in Europe.

Market share

Tesla accounted for about 55 percent of battery electric vehicle sales in the United States in 2023, down from more than 70 percent in 2020, and roughly 4 percent of total U.S. light-vehicle sales. Globally it was overtaken by China's BYD in battery electric volume in the fourth quarter of 2023 and for the full year 2024, as competition from Chinese manufacturers and legacy automakers intensified.

Volcano

A volcano is an opening in the crust of a planetary body through which molten rock, volcanic ash, and gases escape from a magma reservoir beneath the surface. The term derives from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire, whose forge was said to lie beneath the island of Vulcano in the Aeolian Islands. Earth has roughly 1,350 potentially active volcanoes on land, of which about 50 to 70 erupt in a typical year, and an estimated 800 million people live within 100 kilometres of one. Volcanism has shaped the planet's atmosphere, oceans, and continents over 4.5 billion years and remains a leading geological hazard.

Plate Tectonics and Distribution

Most volcanoes occur along the boundaries of Earth's lithospheric plates, a relationship explained by the theory of plate tectonics developed in the 1960s from earlier ideas of Alfred Wegener (1912) and Harry Hess (1962). At divergent boundaries such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, plates separate and mantle rock rises and partially melts by decompression, producing basalt. Roughly three-quarters of Earth's annual magma output, about 20 cubic kilometres, erupts at mid-ocean ridges, mostly unseen beneath the sea; Iceland is the main place where a ridge rises above sea level. At convergent boundaries, an oceanic plate descends into the mantle in a subduction zone, releasing water that lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge. The resulting arc volcanoes form the Pacific Ring of Fire, a 40,000-kilometre belt containing about 75 per cent of the world's active volcanoes, including those of Japan, Indonesia, Kamchatka, the Andes, and the Cascades. A third category, intraplate or hotspot volcanism, was proposed by J. Tuzo Wilson in 1963 to explain the Hawaiian–Emperor chain, in which the Pacific Plate moves northwest at about 7 to 10 centimetres per year over a fixed mantle plume, producing a line of progressively older islands. Yellowstone, the Galápagos, and Réunion are other hotspot examples.

Magma Types

Magma composition is classified chiefly by silica (SiO2) content, which controls viscosity and therefore eruptive behaviour. Basaltic magma contains 45 to 52 per cent silica, erupts at 1,000 to 1,200 degrees Celsius, and is fluid, allowing dissolved gases to escape readily. Andesitic magma (52 to 63 per cent silica), named for the Andes, is intermediate. Dacitic (63 to 69 per cent) and rhyolitic (above 69 per cent) magmas erupt at 650 to 900 degrees Celsius and are highly viscous, trapping gas and favouring explosive eruptions. The principal volcanic gases are water vapour (typically 70 to 90 per cent), carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, hydrogen sulphide, and hydrogen chloride. Norman Bowen's reaction series, published in 1928, describes how fractional crystallisation of minerals such as olivine and pyroxene from a cooling basaltic melt drives the residual liquid toward silica-rich compositions.

Eruption Styles

Eruptions are commonly described by styles named after type localities. Hawaiian eruptions produce lava fountains and fluid flows of pahoehoe and aa lava. Strombolian activity, after Stromboli in Italy, which has erupted almost continuously for about 2,000 years, consists of rhythmic bursts of incandescent cinders every few minutes. Vulcanian eruptions are discrete, cannon-like explosions ejecting blocks and ash. Plinian eruptions, named for Pliny the Younger's account of Vesuvius in AD 79, generate sustained columns of ash and gas 20 to 50 kilometres high. Phreatomagmatic eruptions result when magma meets groundwater or seawater, as at Surtsey, Iceland, in 1963. The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI), devised by Chris Newhall and Stephen Self in 1982, ranks eruptions logarithmically from 0 to 8 by erupted volume; a VEI 8 event ejects more than 1,000 cubic kilometres.

The deadliest volcanic phenomena are pyroclastic density currents, avalanches of hot gas and ash moving at 100 to 700 kilometres per hour at temperatures up to 1,000 degrees Celsius, and lahars, volcanic mudflows that can travel more than 100 kilometres down river valleys. Volcanoes themselves are classified by form: shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa, which rises about 9 kilometres from the sea floor; stratovolcanoes or composite cones such as Fuji and Mount Rainier; cinder cones such as Parícutin, which grew from a Mexican cornfield beginning on 20 February 1943; and calderas, large collapse depressions such as Crater Lake, Oregon, formed about 7,700 years ago.

Famous Eruptions

Vesuvius erupted on 24 August (or possibly October) AD 79, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under up to 25 metres of ash and pyroclastic deposits; roughly 2,000 bodies have been recovered, and the total death toll is estimated at 16,000. Pliny the Elder, commanding the Roman fleet at Misenum, died during the rescue attempt. The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia in April 1815, a VEI 7 event and the largest in recorded history, killed about 10,000 people directly and a further 60,000 to 90,000 through famine and disease; its sulphate aerosols lowered global temperatures by about 0.5 degrees Celsius, causing the 1816 "Year Without a Summer" and crop failures across Europe and North America. Krakatau, between Java and Sumatra, erupted on 26 and 27 August 1883 with explosions heard 4,800 kilometres away; the resulting tsunamis, up to 36 metres high, killed an estimated 36,417 people.

Mount Pelée on Martinique destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre on 8 May 1902 in a pyroclastic surge that killed about 28,000 people in minutes, leaving a handful of survivors including the prisoner Ludger Sylbaris, protected by his cell. Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia produced lahars on 13 November 1985 that buried the town of Armero and killed about 23,000. Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted on 18 May 1980 after a magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the largest landslide in recorded history, killing 57 people including volcanologist David Johnston and resident Harry Truman. Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991, the second-largest eruption of the twentieth century; timely evacuation of some 60,000 people held the death toll to about 850, though 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide cooled the globe by around 0.5 degrees for two years. Unzen in Japan killed 43 people on 3 June 1991, including the volcanologists Maurice and Katia Krafft and Harry Glicken. Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland in April 2010 killed no one but closed European airspace for six days, affecting 10 million travellers. The submarine eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai on 15 January 2022 sent a plume 57 kilometres into the mesosphere and caused tsunamis that killed at least six people. The Laki fissure eruption in Iceland in 1783–1784 released about 120 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide, killing roughly a fifth of Iceland's population and possibly tens of thousands in Europe through poisoned air.

Monitoring and Prediction

Modern volcanology dates from the founding of the Vesuvius Observatory in 1841 and the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory by Thomas Jaggar in 1912. Monitoring combines seismometers, which detect the harmonic tremor and swarms of small earthquakes caused by rising magma; GPS receivers and tiltmeters, which measure ground deformation of a few millimetres; satellite radar interferometry (InSAR); gas spectrometers measuring sulphur dioxide flux; and thermal imaging. The Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program maintains the standard catalogue of Holocene volcanoes. Successful forecasts, such as at Pinatubo in 1991 and Merapi in 2010, have saved tens of thousands of lives, though the exact timing of eruptions remains difficult to predict.

Volcanic Soils and Benefits

Weathered volcanic ash produces andisols, soils rich in phosphorus, potassium, and trace elements with high water-holding capacity, which support dense populations on Java, in Central America, around Naples, and on the slopes of Etna. Geothermal energy from volcanic regions supplies about 25 per cent of Iceland's electricity and nearly all of its space heating, and New Zealand, Kenya, and the Philippines are major producers. Volcanic processes concentrate copper, gold, silver, and sulphur in ore deposits, while pumice, obsidian, basalt, and tuff have been quarried since antiquity. Volcanoes also sustain tourism and, over geological time, released much of the water and carbon dioxide that formed Earth's oceans and atmosphere.

Association Football

Association football, commonly known as football or soccer, is a team sport played between two sides of eleven players using a spherical ball. It is the most widely played and watched sport in the world, with an estimated 250 million players in more than 200 countries and a global television audience for its quadrennial World Cup final that FIFA has claimed exceeds one billion viewers.

Origins in England

Ball games involving kicking are recorded in ancient China (cuju, from the Han dynasty), Greece, Rome and medieval Europe, but the modern codified sport emerged in nineteenth-century England. Folk football, played between villages with few rules and considerable violence, was repeatedly banned by English monarchs from Edward II in 1314 onward. In the early 1800s, public schools such as Eton, Harrow, Rugby and Winchester developed their own written codes. The Cambridge Rules of 1848, drafted at Trinity College by representatives of several schools, attempted a compromise, as did the rules adopted at Sheffield Football Club, founded in 1857 and the oldest surviving club.

On 26 October 1863, representatives of twelve London clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in Great Queen Street and formed the Football Association (FA), the first governing body of the sport. Over six meetings, the FA settled on rules that prohibited carrying the ball and "hacking" (kicking opponents' shins), prompting the withdrawal of Blackheath and the eventual separate codification of rugby football in 1871. The FA Cup, the oldest surviving competition, was first contested in 1871–72 and won by Wanderers, who beat Royal Engineers 1–0 at the Kennington Oval. The first international match, Scotland against England, was played at Hamilton Crescent, Glasgow, on 30 November 1872 and ended 0–0. The Football League, the first national league, was founded in 1888 by Aston Villa director William McGregor with twelve clubs; Preston North End won the inaugural title unbeaten. Professionalism, long resisted by the FA, was legalised in 1885.

Laws of the Game

The sport is governed by the seventeen Laws of the Game, maintained since 1886 by the International Football Association Board (IFAB), composed of the four British associations, which hold four votes, and FIFA, which holds four; changes require six of eight votes. The laws cover the field of play (100–110 m long and 64–75 m wide for international matches), the ball (circumference 68–70 cm, weight 410–450 g), the number of players, equipment, the referee and other officials, duration (two halves of 45 minutes), offside, fouls and misconduct, free kicks, penalties, throw-ins, goal kicks and corner kicks.

Notable amendments include the introduction of the penalty kick in 1891, proposed by Irish goalkeeper William McCrum; the 1925 change to the offside law reducing the number of defenders required from three to two, which immediately increased goals from 4,700 to 6,373 in the English league; the legalisation of substitutes in 1958 and their adoption in the Football League in 1965; red and yellow cards, devised by English referee Ken Aston and first used at the 1970 World Cup; the back-pass rule of 1992; and the video assistant referee (VAR), approved by IFAB in March 2018 and used at that year's World Cup in Russia.

FIFA

The Fédération Internationale de Football Association was founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 by representatives of Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland, with Robert Guérin as first president. The British associations joined in 1905 but withdrew twice, between 1920 and 1924 and again from 1928 to 1946, over disputes about playing wartime enemies and payments to amateurs. FIFA is headquartered in Zurich and comprises 211 member associations organised into six confederations: UEFA (Europe), CONMEBOL (South America), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean), CAF (Africa), AFC (Asia) and OFC (Oceania). Its presidents have included Jules Rimet (1921–54), Stanley Rous (1961–74), João Havelange (1974–98), Sepp Blatter (1998–2015) and Gianni Infantino (since 2016). FIFA reported revenue of US$7.6 billion for the 2019–22 cycle.

World Cup History and Records

Football was included at the Olympic Games from 1900 and became an official medal sport in 1908, but FIFA, under Rimet, organised its own World Cup, first held in Uruguay in 1930 to coincide with the host's centenary of independence. Thirteen teams took part, only four from Europe owing to the length of the sea voyage. Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2 in the final in Montevideo's Estadio Centenario before roughly 68,000 spectators. The tournament has been held every four years except 1942 and 1946, cancelled because of the Second World War.

Brazil has won a record five titles (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002); Germany and Italy have four each; Argentina three; Uruguay and France two; and England and Spain one. The 1950 final-round match in which Uruguay beat hosts Brazil 2–1 at the Maracanã, before an officially recorded 173,850 spectators, is known as the Maracanazo. Pelé remains the only player to win three World Cups. Miroslav Klose of Germany holds the record of 16 tournament goals; Just Fontaine of France scored 13 in a single tournament in 1958. Lionel Messi has made a record 26 appearances. Germany's 7–1 semi-final win over Brazil in 2014 is the heaviest defeat of a host nation. The 2022 tournament in Qatar, the first in the Arab world and the first played in November and December, concluded with Argentina beating France on penalties after a 3–3 draw, with Kylian Mbappé scoring a hat-trick. The 2026 edition, hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, will expand from 32 to 48 teams.

The Women's Game

Women played organised matches in Britain from the 1890s; the British Ladies' Football Club, led by Nettie Honeyball, played its first game in 1895. During the First World War, works teams such as Dick, Kerr Ladies of Preston drew large crowds, including 53,000 at Goodison Park on 26 December 1920. On 5 December 1921, the FA banned women from playing on affiliated grounds, calling the game "quite unsuitable for females"; the ban remained until 1971. UEFA held its first women's championship in 1984, and the first FIFA Women's World Cup took place in China in 1991, won by the United States. The United States has won four titles (1991, 1999, 2015, 2019), Germany two, and Norway, Japan and Spain one each. The 1999 final at the Rose Bowl drew 90,185 spectators. The 2023 tournament in Australia and New Zealand, expanded to 32 teams, attracted nearly two million spectators. A 91,553 crowd at the Camp Nou for a Barcelona–Wolfsburg Champions League semi-final in April 2022 set a record for a women's club match. Disputes over equal pay led the US Soccer Federation to agree a US$24 million settlement with its women's players in 2022.

Money and Transfer Fees

The first four-figure transfer was Alf Common's £1,000 move from Sunderland to Middlesbrough in 1905. Subsequent landmarks include Trevor Francis becoming the first £1 million British player in 1979, Diego Maradona's £6.9 million move to Napoli in 1984, Zinedine Zidane's €77.5 million transfer to Real Madrid in 2001, and Neymar's €222 million transfer from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain in August 2017, still the record. The 1995 Bosman ruling by the European Court of Justice allowed players to move freely at the end of contracts and abolished UEFA quotas on foreign EU players. England's Premier League, formed in 1992, sold domestic television rights for £5 billion for 2022–25. Deloitte estimated European football's market at €35 billion in 2022–23, with Real Madrid the first club to exceed €1 billion in annual revenue. Concerns over debt, state ownership of clubs such as Manchester City and Newcastle United, and the aborted European Super League of April 2021 have fuelled debate over financial regulation, including UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules introduced in 2011.

Governance Scandals

FIFA's governance has been repeatedly discredited. Havelange's and Blatter's eras were marked by allegations surrounding the marketing company ISL, which collapsed in 2001 after paying an estimated CHF 140 million in bribes. On 27 May 2015, Swiss police arrested seven FIFA officials in Zurich at the request of the US Department of Justice, which indicted 14 individuals on racketeering, wire fraud and money-laundering charges totalling more than US$150 million; among those later convicted were CONCACAF president Jeffrey Webb and former FIFA vice-president Jack Warner's associates. Blatter resigned days after re-election and, together with UEFA president Michel Platini, was banned for eight years (later reduced) over a CHF 2 million "disloyal payment"; both were acquitted of fraud by a Swiss court in 2022. The 2010 vote awarding the 2018 and 2022 World Cups to Russia and Qatar prompted the Garcia Report, whose summary FIFA initially refused to publish in full. Qatar's preparations drew criticism from human-rights organisations over the deaths of migrant workers under the kafala system; the Guardian reported 6,500 deaths of South Asian workers in the country between 2010 and 2021, a figure the Qatari government disputed. Match-fixing scandals, including Italy's Calciopoli affair of 2006, which saw Juventus stripped of two titles and relegated, and corruption in the game's broadcasting and sponsorship markets, remain continuing concerns.

Minecraft

Minecraft is a sandbox video game developed by the Swedish studio Mojang Studios. Created by Markus "Notch" Persson and first released as a public alpha in May 2009, it became the best-selling video game in history, with more than 300 million copies sold by October 2023. The game places players in a procedurally generated world composed of cubic blocks, which can be mined, collected and placed to construct structures of nearly unlimited complexity. Since 2014 the intellectual property has been owned by Microsoft, which acquired Mojang for US$2.5 billion.

Development history

Persson, a programmer who had worked at King.com and jAlbum, began developing Minecraft in early 2009, drawing on Infiniminer, Dwarf Fortress, Dungeon Keeper and RollerCoaster Tycoon as influences. He posted the first version, then called "Cave Game," to the TIGSource forums on 17 May 2009; the name "Minecraft" was adopted shortly afterward. The game was written in Java using the Lightweight Java Game Library, and Persson sold it directly from his website for roughly 10 euros during the alpha period, with a promise of free updates thereafter.

Persson founded Mojang AB in September 2010 with Jakob Porsér and Carl Manneh after the game's revenue allowed him to leave his day job. Minecraft entered beta on 20 December 2010, and the full version 1.0 was released on 18 November 2011 at the first MineCon convention in Las Vegas. By that point Persson had handed lead development to Jens "Jeb" Bergensten, who became the game's lead designer in December 2011 and has remained in that role since.

A series of major updates followed: the Adventure Update (1.0), the Redstone Update (1.5, 2013), the Bountiful Update (1.8, 2014), the Combat Update (1.9, 2016), Update Aquatic (1.13, 2018), Village and Pillage (1.14, 2019), the Nether Update (1.16, 2020), Caves and Cliffs (1.17 and 1.18, 2021), the Wild Update (1.19, 2022), Trails and Tales (1.20, 2023) and Tricky Trials (1.21, 2024). Ports to Xbox 360 (2012), mobile platforms (Pocket Edition, 2011), PlayStation 3 (2013) and later consoles were developed by 4J Studios and Mojang. In 2017 the "Better Together" update unified the Windows 10, mobile, Xbox One and Nintendo Switch versions into a single C++ codebase known as Bedrock Edition, distinct from the original Java Edition, which continues to be maintained in parallel.

Sale to Microsoft

On 15 September 2014, Microsoft announced it would acquire Mojang for US$2.5 billion. Persson had publicly expressed exhaustion with the responsibilities of ownership, tweeting in June 2014, "Anyone want to buy my share of Mojang so I can move on with my life?" Persson, Porsér and Manneh left the company upon completion of the deal on 6 November 2014. Persson's share was estimated at around US$1.75 billion; he subsequently purchased a US$70 million mansion in Beverly Hills. Microsoft placed the studio within its Xbox Game Studios division, and Mojang AB was renamed Mojang Studios in May 2020. Persson's name and references to him were removed from the game's splash screens and credits in March 2019 following a series of controversial statements on social media, discussed below.

Game modes

Minecraft offers several modes. Survival mode requires players to gather resources, manage health and hunger, craft tools, and defend against hostile mobs such as zombies, skeletons, creepers and endermen, which spawn in darkness. A day-night cycle lasts 20 real-time minutes. Hardcore mode is a Survival variant locked to the highest difficulty in which death is permanent and the world is deleted or made spectator-only. Creative mode grants unlimited blocks, flight and invulnerability, and is primarily used for building. Adventure mode, added in 2012, restricts block breaking and placing to support custom maps, and Spectator mode (2014) allows non-interactive observation.

Worlds extend horizontally for roughly 30 million blocks in each direction and, since the Caves and Cliffs update, span 384 vertical blocks from Y=-64 to Y=320. Two additional dimensions exist: the Nether, a hellish realm accessed through obsidian portals, and the End, home to the Ender Dragon, whose defeat triggers the game's end credits. Multiplayer is supported through player-hosted servers, Mojang's paid Realms service, and, for Bedrock, featured partner servers such as Hypixel, which has recorded over 200,000 concurrent players.

Sales figures and commercial performance

Minecraft reached one million sales in January 2011 while still in beta and 10 million by April 2013. Mojang reported 100 million copies across platforms in June 2016, 176 million in May 2019, 200 million in May 2020, 238 million in April 2021 and 300 million in October 2023, with roughly 140 million monthly active players at the later date. Mojang reported revenue of approximately US$330 million in 2014, the year of the acquisition. The Minecraft Marketplace, launched in 2017 for Bedrock Edition, had paid out over US$350 million to third-party creators by 2021. Spin-offs include Minecraft: Story Mode (Telltale Games, 2015), Minecraft Dungeons (2020), Minecraft Earth (2019–2021) and Minecraft Legends (2023). A live-action film, A Minecraft Movie, directed by Jared Hess and starring Jack Black and Jason Momoa, was released by Warner Bros. in April 2025 and grossed over US$950 million worldwide.

Education Edition

MinecraftEdu, a modification created by the Finnish company TeacherGaming in 2011, was acquired by Microsoft in January 2016 and relaunched as Minecraft: Education Edition in November 2016. It includes classroom management tools, a chemistry resource pack, a code builder supporting Python and Microsoft MakeCode, and lesson plans aligned with curricula in subjects from history to computer science. It is licensed per user at about US$5 annually and was used by more than 35 million licensed educators and students across 115 countries by 2020. During the COVID-19 pandemic Mojang made educational content free to download for Java and Bedrock users through June 2020.

Redstone

Redstone, an ore introduced in the alpha version in July 2010, functions as the game's electrical system. Redstone dust transmits a signal up to 15 blocks, and components such as repeaters, comparators, pistons, observers, hoppers and droppers allow players to construct logic gates and complex machines. Because redstone circuits can implement NOT, AND and OR gates, the system is Turing complete. Players have built functioning calculators, 8-bit and 16-bit processors, a word processor, a playable version of Minecraft running inside Minecraft, and in 2022 a graphical computer with a 32-bit CPU capable of running Tetris. Redstone engineering is widely used in educational contexts to teach digital logic.

Community controversies

Minecraft's community has generated numerous controversies. Persson drew criticism between 2017 and 2019 for tweets endorsing conspiracy theories including QAnon and Pizzagate, making transphobic remarks, and stating that "it's ok to be white," leading Microsoft to exclude him from the game's tenth-anniversary celebrations in 2019.

The End User License Agreement was revised in 2014 to prohibit servers from selling gameplay-affecting items for real money, provoking backlash from server operators who relied on such sales. In 2022 Mojang introduced the Player Reporting system and a Chat Reporting feature in Java Edition 1.19.1, allowing players to be banned from all multiplayer servers for reported messages; a protest campaign under the slogan "No Chat Reports" led many server operators to disable the feature.

Several prominent community figures have faced abuse allegations. In 2019 and 2020, YouTubers including Mini Ladd and CallMeCarson were accused of inappropriate conduct with minors. Dream, among the most popular Minecraft content creators with over 30 million subscribers, was found in 2020 by a team of moderators to have used a modified game in speedruns submitted to speedrun.com; he later admitted the modification was active but denied intent. In 2022 and 2024 he faced further allegations of grooming, which he denied, and the game's broader streaming culture has been criticized for the exposure of young audiences to such disputes. Mojang itself was criticized in 2021 for removing a planned mob, the fireflies, and for the decision to split the Caves and Cliffs update, while the 2023 "mob vote" prompted a petition with more than 500,000 signatures calling for its abolition.

Honey Bee

The honey bee (genus Apis) is a eusocial flying insect of the family Apidae, best known for producing and storing honey and for constructing perennial colonial nests from wax. Of the roughly 20,000 described bee species, only seven to twelve are recognized as honey bees, all native to Eurasia and Africa. The western honey bee, Apis mellifera, described by Carl Linnaeus in 1758, is the most widely distributed managed pollinator in the world, having been introduced to the Americas in the early 1620s, to Australia in 1822, and to New Zealand in 1839. Other species include the eastern honey bee (Apis cerana), the giant honey bee (Apis dorsata), and the dwarf honey bee (Apis florea). A fossil of Apis nearctica from Nevada indicates that honey bees existed in North America about 14 million years ago before going extinct there.

Colony Castes

A honey bee colony typically contains 20,000 to 80,000 individuals divided into three castes. A single queen is the sole fertile female and lays up to 1,500 to 2,000 eggs per day at the height of spring, exceeding her own body weight daily. She develops from a fertilized egg reared in an enlarged vertical cell and fed exclusively on royal jelly, a glandular secretion; the same egg fed a mixed diet of pollen and nectar would become a worker. Queens emerge after 16 days of development and may live two to five years. Within a week of emergence a virgin queen undertakes one or more mating flights to drone congregation areas, mating with an average of 12 drones at altitudes of 10 to 40 meters and storing about five to six million sperm in her spermatheca for life.

Workers are sterile females developing in 21 days. They live roughly six weeks in summer but four to six months when reared in autumn. Their tasks are age-related: cell cleaning in the first days, nursing larvae from about day 3 to 11, wax secretion and comb building from day 12 to 17, guarding and ventilating thereafter, and foraging from about three weeks until death. Workers possess barbed stingers that lodge in mammalian skin, tearing free with the venom sac and killing the bee. Drones, the males, develop from unfertilized eggs in 24 days, lack stingers, and exist to mate. A drone dies within minutes of mating as his endophallus is ripped from his body. In temperate regions workers expel surviving drones from the hive in autumn, where they starve.

Communication and the Waggle Dance

Foragers communicate the location of food sources through the waggle dance, decoded by the Austrian ethologist Karl von Frisch, whose work beginning in the 1920s earned him a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. A returning forager performs a figure-eight pattern on the vertical comb; during the straight waggle run she vibrates her abdomen at about 13 Hz. The angle of the run relative to vertical corresponds to the direction of the source relative to the sun's azimuth, and the run's duration encodes distance, roughly 75 milliseconds per 100 meters in A. mellifera. Sources closer than about 50 to 100 meters elicit a round dance lacking directional information. Von Frisch's findings were disputed by Adrian Wenner in the 1960s, who argued odor was primary; experiments by James Gould in 1975 and robotic dancers in the 1980s confirmed the dance conveys directional information. Workers also communicate by pheromones, including queen mandibular pheromone, which suppresses worker ovary development, and the alarm pheromone isopentyl acetate, released when a bee stings.

Honey Production

Nectar collected from flowers is carried in the forager's honey stomach, which holds about 40 milligrams, and transferred to house bees by trophallaxis. Enzymes, chiefly invertase, break sucrose into glucose and fructose, and workers fan the nectar to reduce its water content from 70 to 80 percent to below 18 percent before capping the cells with wax. The resulting honey is about 38 percent fructose, 31 percent glucose, and 17 percent water, with a pH near 3.9; its low water activity and hydrogen peroxide generated by glucose oxidase make it resistant to spoilage. A colony requires roughly 25 to 40 kilograms of honey to overwinter in a cold climate and may produce a surplus of 25 to 50 kilograms for the beekeeper. To make one kilogram of honey, bees visit about four million flowers and fly a cumulative distance of roughly 150,000 kilometers. World production was about 1.8 million tonnes in 2021, with China the largest producer at over 470,000 tonnes, followed by Turkey, Iran, and Argentina. Wax, propolis, royal jelly, and pollen are also harvested commercially.

Pollination and Agricultural Value

Honey bees pollinate an estimated one-third of crop types by volume, including almonds, apples, blueberries, cherries, melons, and cucurbits. In 2000 Roger Morse and Nicholas Calderone estimated the value of honey bee pollination to United States agriculture at 14.6 billion dollars annually; a 2012 study estimated 15 to 20 billion dollars. Globally, pollinator-dependent crops were valued at 235 to 577 billion dollars per year by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services in 2016. California's almond industry, covering over 1.3 million acres, requires about 2 million hives each February, the largest managed pollination event in the world, drawing roughly 85 percent of the United States' commercial colonies and generating rental fees of 180 to 200 dollars per hive.

Varroa Mites and Disease

The parasitic mite Varroa destructor, described as a distinct species by Denis Anderson and John Trueman in 2000, is the most damaging pest of A. mellifera. Native to Asia, where its original host A. cerana tolerates it, the mite reached the Soviet Union in the 1960s, Western Europe in the 1970s, the United States in 1987, and New Zealand in 2000; Australia reported its first established population in June 2022. Adult female mites, about 1.1 by 1.5 millimeters, enter brood cells before capping and reproduce on the developing pupa, feeding on the fat body. Untreated colonies usually die within one to three years. Varroa also transmits deformed wing virus and acute bee paralysis virus, and mite-borne viral loads are implicated in most winter losses. Treatments include the synthetic acaricides fluvalinate and amitraz, against which resistance has evolved, and organic compounds such as formic acid, oxalic acid, and thymol. Other pathogens include the microsporidian Nosema ceranae, the bacterial brood diseases American foulbrood (Paenibacillus larvae) and European foulbrood, the tracheal mite Acarapis woodi, and the small hive beetle Aethina tumida.

Colony Collapse Disorder

In late 2006 the Pennsylvania beekeeper David Hackenberg reported the sudden loss of adult bees from hives containing a live queen, brood, and food stores, with no accumulation of dead bees. The syndrome was named colony collapse disorder in 2007 by researchers including Dennis vanEngelsdorp and Diana Cox-Foster. United States beekeepers lost about 32 percent of colonies in the winter of 2006 to 2007 and over 35 percent the following winter. No single cause was identified; studies implicated interactions among varroa, viruses, Nosema, poor nutrition from monoculture, and pesticides, particularly neonicotinoid insecticides such as imidacloprid and clothianidin, which the European Union restricted on flowering crops in 2013 and banned outdoors in 2018. Classic CCD symptoms became rare after 2010, but annual losses in the United States have remained between 30 and 45 percent, driven mainly by varroa.

Beekeeping History

Rock paintings at the Cuevas de la Araña near Valencia, Spain, dated to roughly 8,000 years ago, depict a figure gathering honey from a wild nest. Egyptian reliefs from the sun temple of Nyuserre at Abu Gurab, about 2400 BCE, show beekeepers working with clay cylinder hives. Hives dating to about 900 BCE were excavated at Tel Rehov in Israel in 2007. Aristotle described bee behavior in the Historia Animalium, and Virgil devoted the fourth book of the Georgics to apiculture. Until the nineteenth century, European beekeepers kept bees in straw skeps and typically killed colonies with sulfur fumes to harvest honey. Jan Dzierżon of Silesia demonstrated drone parthenogenesis in 1845, and the American clergyman Lorenzo Lorraine Langstroth patented the movable-frame hive in 1852, based on the "bee space" of about 9.5 millimeters, which bees neither fill with comb nor seal with propolis. Johannes Mehring invented comb foundation in 1857, and Franz von Hruschka introduced the centrifugal extractor in 1865. The Buckfast bee was bred by Brother Adam at Buckfast Abbey in Devon beginning in 1919 for resistance to tracheal mites. Africanized honey bees, hybrids escaped from Warwick Kerr's breeding program in Brazil in 1957, reached Texas in 1990. About 100 million managed colonies exist worldwide today.

Black Hole

A black hole is a region of spacetime in which gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it. The boundary of this region is called the event horizon. Black holes are predicted by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, published in 1915, and are now understood to be common objects in the universe, forming from the collapse of massive stars and residing at the centres of most large galaxies.

Theoretical Background

The idea of a body so massive that light could not escape it was first proposed by the English clergyman John Michell in 1783 and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1796, using Newtonian mechanics. The modern concept emerged from general relativity. In 1916, only months after Einstein's field equations appeared, the German physicist Karl Schwarzschild, serving on the Eastern Front, derived the first exact solution describing the gravitational field outside a spherical, non-rotating mass. The solution contains a characteristic distance, the Schwarzschild radius, given by 2GM/c², where G is the gravitational constant, M the mass and c the speed of light. For the Sun this radius is about 3 kilometres; for the Earth, about 9 millimetres.

For decades the singular behaviour at the Schwarzschild radius was regarded as a mathematical artefact. In 1939 J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder showed that a sufficiently massive collapsing star would inevitably contract within its Schwarzschild radius. Interest revived in the 1960s with work by Roger Penrose, who in 1965 proved that gravitational collapse under general conditions leads to a singularity, a result for which he shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics. The term "black hole" was popularised by the American physicist John Archibald Wheeler in 1967. Roy Kerr found the solution for a rotating black hole in 1963, and the Kerr metric is now considered the generic astrophysical case, since nearly all collapsing objects possess angular momentum.

Event Horizon and Singularity

The event horizon is a surface of no return rather than a physical membrane. An observer falling through the horizon of a large black hole would notice nothing special locally, but no signal emitted from inside can reach the outside. To a distant observer, an infalling object appears to slow down, redden and fade as it approaches the horizon, never quite seen to cross it, an effect of gravitational time dilation. Inside the horizon, general relativity predicts that all matter is crushed toward a central singularity of infinite density, where the theory itself breaks down. Near a stellar-mass black hole, tidal forces, the difference in gravitational pull between a body's near and far sides, would stretch an infalling object lengthwise while compressing it sideways, a process informally termed spaghettification. For supermassive black holes, tidal forces at the horizon are comparatively gentle.

According to the "no-hair" theorem, developed by Werner Israel, Brandon Carter and others in the late 1960s and early 1970s, a stationary black hole is completely described by just three externally observable quantities: mass, electric charge and angular momentum.

Stellar-Mass Black Holes

Stellar-mass black holes, typically between about 3 and 100 solar masses, form when stars of more than roughly 20 solar masses exhaust their nuclear fuel. The core collapses, often accompanied by a supernova explosion, and if the remnant exceeds the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit, about 2 to 3 solar masses, neutron degeneracy pressure cannot halt the collapse. The first strong candidate was Cygnus X-1, an X-ray source discovered in 1964 and identified in 1971 by Charles Thomas Bolton, Louise Webster and Paul Murdin as a compact object orbiting a blue supergiant. Its mass is now estimated at about 21 solar masses. Such systems are detected because gas pulled from a companion star forms an accretion disc that heats to millions of degrees and emits X-rays. The Milky Way is estimated to contain some 100 million stellar-mass black holes, the overwhelming majority undetected.

Supermassive Black Holes and Sagittarius A*

Supermassive black holes, with masses from about one million to tens of billions of solar masses, are found at the centres of most galaxies. Their origin remains debated; proposals include the growth of stellar remnants by accretion and mergers, and the direct collapse of gas clouds in the early universe. The quasar 3C 273, identified by Maarten Schmidt in 1963, was the first object recognised as powered by accretion onto such a black hole. The most massive known include TON 618, estimated at roughly 40 billion solar masses.

The Milky Way's central black hole, Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), lies about 26,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Sagittarius. The compact radio source was discovered by Bruce Balick and Robert Brown in 1974. From the 1990s onward, teams led by Reinhard Genzel at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics and Andrea Ghez at the University of California, Los Angeles tracked individual stars orbiting the galactic centre using infrared telescopes. The star S2, which completes an orbit every 16 years and approaches within about 120 astronomical units of the centre, moving at nearly 3 percent of the speed of light, allowed the mass to be measured at about 4.3 million solar masses. Genzel and Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics with Penrose for this work.

The Event Horizon Telescope Images

On 10 April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration, comprising more than 200 scientists, released the first direct image of a black hole's immediate environment. The target was the supermassive black hole at the centre of the elliptical galaxy Messier 87 (M87*), about 55 million light-years away, with a mass of some 6.5 billion solar masses. The EHT combined eight radio observatories across four continents, from Hawaii to the South Pole, through very-long-baseline interferometry, achieving an angular resolution of about 20 microarcseconds, comparable to reading a newspaper in New York from Paris. The image, built from data collected in April 2017, shows a dark central shadow about 40 microarcseconds across surrounded by a bright asymmetric ring of emission from hot gas. The processing of the data was led in part by Katie Bouman and Kazunori Akiyama. On 12 May 2022 the collaboration published a comparable image of Sgr A*, whose smaller size and rapidly varying emission had made imaging more difficult.

Gravitational Waves

General relativity predicts that accelerating masses emit ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves. On 14 September 2015 the two detectors of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), in Hanford, Washington, and Livingston, Louisiana, recorded a signal designated GW150914, announced on 11 February 2016. It was produced by the merger of two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses, approximately 1.3 billion light-years away, forming a single black hole of 62 solar masses; the remaining 3 solar masses were radiated as gravitational-wave energy within a fraction of a second. The detectors, each with 4-kilometre arms, measured a change in length of less than one ten-thousandth the diameter of a proton. Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics. By 2023 LIGO and its European partner Virgo had catalogued more than 90 merger events.

Hawking Radiation

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that quantum effects near the event horizon cause black holes to emit thermal radiation, with a temperature inversely proportional to mass. For a solar-mass black hole the temperature is about 60 billionths of a kelvin, far below the 2.7 kelvin cosmic microwave background, so such objects currently absorb more than they radiate. A stellar black hole would take roughly 10⁶⁷ years to evaporate. The result built on Jacob Bekenstein's 1972 proposal that black holes possess entropy proportional to horizon area and raised the "information paradox", the question of whether information falling into a black hole is destroyed, which remains unresolved. Hawking radiation has not been observed directly.

Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, 2025

The 2025 Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race was the 53rd running of the long-distance sled dog race held annually in Alaska. It was won by Jessie Holmes of Nenana, who reached the burled-arch finish line in Nome in the early hours of March 14, 2025. The race was notable for being contested over the longest course in its history, for having the smallest starting field ever recorded, and for renewed public debate over the treatment of the dogs that compete in it.

Background

The Iditarod commemorates the 1925 serum run to Nome, in which relay teams of dog mushers carried diphtheria antitoxin across the territory, and it has been held every year since 1973. The modern race traditionally begins with a ceremonial start in Anchorage on the first Saturday in March, followed by a competitive restart in Willow the next day. Teams then travel roughly 1,000 miles across the Alaska Range, through Interior river villages and along the Bering Sea coast to Nome. The race is organized by the Iditarod Trail Committee, a non-profit based in Wasilla, and is overseen in the field by a race marshal and a staff of volunteer veterinarians led by chief veterinarian Dr. Stuart Nelson.

Course Change and Weather Problems

The 2025 race was shaped before it began by an unusually warm, dry winter in Southcentral Alaska. By late February the trail between Willow and the Alaska Range lacked sufficient snow cover, and sections of the Farewell Burn and the Dalzell Gorge were reported to be bare ground, exposed rock and open water. On February 10, 2025, the Iditarod Trail Committee announced that the competitive restart would be moved about 360 miles north to Fairbanks, a step previously taken in 2003, 2015 and 2017.

The Fairbanks route followed the Chena, Tanana and Yukon rivers westward before rejoining the traditional trail at Kaltag and continuing to the coast. Because organizers also added an out-and-back loop on the Yukon to preserve the race's mileage, the official distance was set at approximately 1,128 miles, the longest in Iditarod history. The ceremonial start in Anchorage was held on March 1 on a shortened downtown course built with trucked-in snow, and the restart took place on March 3 at Pike's Landing in Fairbanks.

Weather continued to affect the race once it was under way. Mushers reported overflow, in which river water rises through cracks and spreads across the ice, on the Tanana and Yukon, along with jumble ice and glare ice that gave dogs poor footing. Later in the race, teams on the Norton Sound coast between Shaktoolik and Koyuk encountered strong winds and ground blizzards, and several mushers chose to hold in checkpoints rather than cross exposed sea ice in low visibility. Temperatures on the Interior rivers fell well below minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit at night in the first week before warming toward the coast.

Field and Winner

Thirty-three mushers started the 2025 race, the smallest field since the event began; the previous low was 38 in 2023. Race officials and participants attributed the decline to the rising cost of maintaining a competitive kennel, reduced sponsorship and a shrinking number of rural mushers.

Jessie Holmes, 43, a carpenter originally from Alabama who moved to Alaska in 2004 and became known to television audiences through the series Life Below Zero, led for much of the second half of the race. He left White Mountain, the final mandatory rest stop 77 miles from Nome, with a lead of several hours over his closest pursuers and arrived at the finish line on Front Street in Nome at about 2:55 a.m. on March 14. His official elapsed time was 10 days, 14 hours, 55 minutes and 41 seconds, with a team of 10 dogs in harness led by Hercules and Polar. The time was slower than recent winning marks, which had fallen below nine days on the standard route, reflecting the greater distance and difficult trail surface. Holmes received a first-place prize of approximately $57,200 from a purse that had been reduced from previous years.

Matt Hall of Two Rivers finished second, about three hours behind, and Paige Drobny of Cantwell was third, the highest finish of her career. Both had been in contention through the Yukon River section. Holmes had previously placed third in 2022 and 2024, and his victory followed a 2024 race in which he and other front-runners had been overshadowed by Dallas Seavey's record sixth win.

Dog Care Rules

Iditarod rules govern team size, rest and veterinary oversight. Teams may start with no more than 14 dogs and must finish with at least five. Each musher is required to take one 24-hour layover at a checkpoint of their choosing, one eight-hour rest at a checkpoint on the Yukon River, and a further eight-hour rest at White Mountain. Before the race, every dog must pass a physical examination, blood work and an electrocardiogram, and dogs are microchipped so that their movement through checkpoints can be tracked.

Roughly 50 volunteer veterinarians staffed the 2025 checkpoints, examining dogs for dehydration, lameness, wrist and shoulder injuries, and signs of pneumonia or gastric ulcers. Mushers carry a veterinary logbook that must be signed at each stop. Dogs that are injured, ill or judged unfit are "dropped" at checkpoints and flown back to Anchorage by the volunteer Iditarod Air Force, where they are cared for until retrieved by handlers. Mushers who abuse a dog, fail to provide adequate food or deliberately avoid veterinary checks may be disqualified. In 2024, Seavey was assessed a two-hour penalty under the rule requiring that a moose killed in self-defense be gutted before the team continues; no comparable incident was reported in 2025.

A Rookie's Story

Among the rookies in the 2025 field was Emily Ford of Duluth, Minnesota, a former chef and long-distance winter trekker who gained attention in 2021 for a solo crossing of Wisconsin's Ice Age Trail and later for an expedition through the Boundary Waters with a borrowed sled dog. Ford moved to Alaska to train with an established kennel and qualified through shorter sanctioned races. She described the Yukon River stretch, with its monotony and extreme cold, as the hardest part of the race, and reported stopping repeatedly to bootie dogs and check for ice-related foot injuries. She finished in Nome in the middle of the field after more than 12 days on the trail and was named Rookie of the Year, receiving a cash award at the finishers' banquet. The final finisher, awarded the traditional Red Lantern, arrived several days after Holmes.

Animal-Welfare Criticism

The race has faced sustained criticism from animal-rights organizations, most prominently People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, which has counted more than 150 dog deaths connected to the Iditarod since 1973 and staged protests at the Anchorage start in 2025. Three dogs died during the 2024 race, the first fatalities since 2019, and one dog died in 2023; critics cited these deaths, along with injuries, frostbite and the culling of unwanted dogs at some kennels, as evidence that the event is inherently harmful. Under pressure from such campaigns, corporate sponsors including Alaska Airlines, Wells Fargo, Jack Daniel's, Coca-Cola and ExxonMobil ended their support between 2017 and 2021.

Race officials and mushers respond that fatalities have declined sharply since the 1990s as veterinary screening has expanded, that mandatory rests and drop procedures protect dogs, and that the animals are bred and conditioned for the work. The 2025 race was completed without a reported dog death on the trail, a fact organizers emphasized in post-race statements, while critics argued that the shrinking field and loss of sponsors reflected a broader public shift away from the sport.
